passage: At the community centre's after-school room, the rain had made every parent late. Five-year-old Yash had not eaten since lunch. He whined at the puzzle, kicked the table leg, then smacked his older brother Chaitanya for touching his crayons. When Chaitanya offered him half a biscuit, it snapped in two, and Yash burst into loud tears. "He's not usually like this," Chaitanya told the helper, Mrs Kamath. She didn't lecture. She fetched a banana and some crackers from the snack tin and sat Yash on a beanbag. Soon he was giggling and sharing his crayons.

qa.q: What happened to the biscuit Chaitanya offered?
qa.a: It snapped in two.

qa.q: Why did Yash burst into tears over the biscuit?
qa.a: He was very hungry, so he felt cross and overwhelmed, and a small upset felt huge.

qa.q: Why did Mrs Kamath's response work?
qa.a: She gave food and a quiet seat instead of a lecture, meeting the physical need behind the mood.

qa.q: What was the afternoon like for Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya got smacked and cried at while trying to help, yet still understood this was not how Yash usually is.

grounding: Shows a young child late for food turning whiny, hitting a sibling and crying over a broken biscuit, and a snack restoring him better than a lecture.

passage: From my balcony I, Bhavna, can see into the Mehtas' courtyard. On Tuesday their dinner ran late; Mrs Mehta was stuck on a work call. Little Deepak, five, went from singing to whining. He yanked his sister's plait, and when she yelled, he threw himself on the steps, wailing that his biscuit had broken "all wrong". Mrs Mehta began a lecture about manners, stopped, and handed him a chapati roll. Soon he was waving up at me. "Bhavna didi, look at my car!" I can't know what was in his head, but the change was hard to miss.

qa.q: Why did dinner run late on Tuesday?
qa.a: Mrs Mehta was stuck on a work call.

qa.q: What might Deepak have been feeling when he threw himself on the steps?
qa.a: He was probably hungry and miserable, so a broken biscuit felt like a disaster.

qa.q: What was wiser than the lecture, and why?
qa.a: Handing him a chapati roll; the mood came from hunger, so food settled him faster than words about manners.

qa.q: How might Deepak's sister see the evening?
qa.a: She had her plait yanked for no reason and may have felt hurt and angry, without knowing he was hungry.

grounding: Illustrates a young child whose late dinner turns him whiny and rough with a sibling, and food restoring him better than a lecture.

passage: At the after-school centre, the clock said six and Trisha's mother was still stuck in traffic. When Trisha's little brother took the red crayon, she hit his arm. Then her biscuit broke in half, and she burst into loud tears. Ganga Aunty didn't give a lecture. She fetched a small bowl of peanuts and banana slices and sat both children on the mat. Trisha ate quietly and sniffed. Then she pushed the red crayon back to her brother.

qa.q: What broke in half?
qa.a: Her biscuit broke in half.

qa.q: Why did Trisha burst into tears over the biscuit?
qa.a: She was very hungry and worn out, so a small upset felt huge and made her cry.

qa.q: Why did Ganga Aunty's snack work better than a lecture?
qa.a: The mood came from hunger, so food settled Trisha's body, and soon she was calm enough to give the crayon back.

qa.q: How might Trisha's brother feel when she hits his arm?
qa.a: He is likely hurt and confused, since he only took a crayon.

grounding: Shows a preschooler late for a meal hitting a sibling and crying over a broken biscuit, and a small snack restoring her.

passage:
Monday: Dinner was at nine because Suraj worked late. At eight, Ishita cried because her doll's shoe fell off, then kicked the sofa. Suraj scolded her, and she cried harder.
Wednesday: Late dinner again. At half past seven Ishita started whining. Suraj remembered Monday. He cut her an apple and poured a glass of milk. She ate on the rug, chatting to her doll.
Friday: At seven, Ishita came into the kitchen by herself. "Papa, my tummy's cross." Suraj laughed and handed her a few crackers.

qa.q: Why was dinner at nine on Monday?
qa.a: Because Suraj worked late.

qa.q: What did Ishita mean by "my tummy's cross"?
qa.a: She was feeling hungry and grumpy, and was starting to recognise that feeling and ask for food.

qa.q: What did Suraj change on Wednesday?
qa.a: Instead of scolding, he gave her an apple and milk before the late dinner, which calmed her.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel on Monday after scolding?
qa.a: He was probably tired and frustrated, and the scolding only made her cry harder.

grounding: Shows a young child falling apart before a late dinner and a small snack restoring her better than scolding.

passage: Rain had flooded the lane, the gas cylinder had run out, and dinner at Farida Nani's house was going to be very late. Aparna, five, had been whining for an hour. When her last biscuit snapped in two, she flung both halves on the floor and wailed, "Everything is broken!" Nani didn't scold. She found a handful of roasted chana in a tin and a banana gone brown at the edges. "Sit with me, gudiya. Eat this while we wait." Aparna chewed, sniffling, head against Nani's arm. By the time a neighbour lent them a stove, she was helping stir the dal.

qa.q: What had run out at Nani's house?
qa.a: The gas cylinder.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she wailed "Everything is broken!"?
qa.a: She was hungry and overwhelmed after a long wait, so the snapped biscuit felt like the last straw.

qa.q: Why did Nani's handful of chana help?
qa.a: It met Aparna's real, physical need quickly, calming her better than a scolding could have while they waited.

qa.q: What might the rainy evening be like for Farida Nani?
qa.a: She is coping with a flooded lane, no gas and a wailing child, yet stays calm and looks for food first.

grounding: Shows a young child late for a meal bursting into tears over a broken biscuit, and a small snack restoring her better than a scolding.

passage: At seven, dinner was still on the stove because Rashmi had come home late from work. Hemant, who had eaten nothing since his school tiffin, whined at every little thing. When his biscuit snapped in half, he burst into tears and hit his little sister's arm. 'Hemant! No hitting!' Rashmi said. He wailed louder. She took a breath, handed him a banana and sat him at the table. 'We'll talk after you eat.' Ten minutes later he patted his sister's arm, said sorry and asked to help lay the plates.

qa.q: What did Rashmi give Hemant?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: Why did Hemant burst into tears over a broken biscuit?
qa.a: He was very hungry, having eaten nothing since his school tiffin, so he felt cranky and small things upset him.

qa.q: Why did 'We'll talk after you eat' work?
qa.a: Food settled Hemant's body first, so he could then say sorry and help, which a lecture couldn't do.

qa.q: How might the little sister have felt when Hemant hit her?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and surprised, until he patted her arm and said sorry.

grounding: A young child whose dinner is late turns whiny and hits, and a small snack restores him better than a lecture.
